item.title: Japan urged to severely punish perpetrator of Chinese embassy break-in: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
Japan urged to severely punish perpetrator of Chinese embassy break-in: spokesperson BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China once again urges the Japanese side to impose severe punishment on the perpetrator who broke into the Chinese Embassy in Japan with a knife to serve as a warning to others, foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Thursday. Mao made the remarks at a regular media briefing while answering a question regarding the first court hearing in the trial of Kodai Murata, a former Japan Self-Defense Forces (SDF) officer accused of forcibly entering the Chinese Embassy in Japan. It is an egregious incident unprecedented in the international community that an active-duty officer of Japan's SDF broke into the Chinese Embassy in Japan with a knife and made violent threats against Chinese diplomatic personnel, Mao said. She said it constitutes a serious violation of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, poses grave threats to the personal safety of Chinese diplomatic staff and the security of the diplomatic premises, and lays bare a host of deep-seated problems in Japan, including rampant right-wing forces and inadequate management and discipline of SDF personnel. "Whether Japan can handle the case seriously in accordance with law will test whether the Japanese government earnestly fulfills its obligations under international law, and bears on the country's national credibility and international image," Mao said. item.title: China warns Philippines to cease provocations, false claims
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
China warns Philippines to cease provocations, false claims BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The China Coast Guard (CCG) on Thursday warned the Philippine side to immediately stop its infringements, provocations and false claims after a Philippine Coast Guard vessel transported an injured person from a grounded vessel near Ren'ai Jiao. Jiang Lue, a spokesperson for the CCG, said that on Thursday, Philippine Coast Guard vessel 4409 went to waters near Ren'ai Jiao to transport one injured person from the vessel illegally grounded there. Out of humanitarian considerations, the Chinese side immediately allowed the Philippine side to transfer the injured person by small boat, and the CCG handled the matter in accordance with the law and regulations, and provided necessary assistance, Jiang said. The Philippine side's relevant remarks disregard the facts and distort the truth in an attempt to mislead the public, Jiang added. China has indisputable sovereignty over the Nansha Qundao, including Ren'ai Jiao, and the adjacent waters, he noted. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Strong demand in China boosts US exporters
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
Strong demand in China boosts US exporters China's growing appetite for high-quality consumer goods and industrial inputs is drawing more products from the United States into its market, as holiday spending, industrial upgrading and the recent reciprocal tariff-cut arrangement offer US exporters more room to expand sales in the country, according to trade experts and business leaders. From fresh fruit and seafood to integrated circuits and energy products, US shipments to China have remained substantial, reflecting the complementary nature of the two economies and the potential for expanding imports to support more balanced and mutually beneficial bilateral trade, they said. The trend was particularly visible during the National Day holiday from Oct 1 to Wednesday, as stronger demand for food and other consumer products prompted Chinese importers to step up purchases from overseas suppliers. Oheng Supply Chain Management (Ningbo) Co, a cross-border food products importer based in Ningbo, Zhejiang province, imported 44.62 million yuan ($6.66 million) worth of products, including fresh cherries and fish oil from the US, in the first eight months of 2026. Ahead of the holiday, shipments of US fish oil, red yeast rice, fresh cherries and grapes purchased by the company arrived in China to replenish supplies for the holiday market. "The US is one of our main sources for products such as fish oil and cherries, with stable supply capacity," said Zhou Shouming, the company's director of customs affairs. "Judging from our sales, domestic consumers' demand for high-quality imported food continues to grow." In late September, China and the US released reciprocal tariff-cut lists covering about $30 billion worth of imports from each side. Zhou said the arrangement will lower costs for products including fresh cherries and grapes and give the company greater flexibility in pricing, allowing it to bring more high-quality US food products to Chinese buyers. Pistachios are also included on China's tariff-cut list. Nut growers in California are expected to export 111,000 metric tons of pistachios to China in the 2026 crop year (Sept 1, 2026 to Aug 31, 2027), according to Wonderful Pistachios & Almonds, the largest pistachio producer by production volume and sales revenue in the US. Anita Lam, managing director for China at Wonderful Pistachios, said the industry remains confident about the long-term growth potential for California pistachios in the Chinese market, adding that her company will continue to leverage its vertically integrated supply chain and long-standing operations to deepen its presence in the country. Demand for fresh seafood has also been strong in China. Imports of US lobsters through Ningbo Lishe International Airport were valued at 200 million yuan between January and August, surging 468.5 percent year-on-year, according to Ningbo Customs. Li Yongguo, president of Hengsheng Supply Chain (Dongguan) Co, a Dongguan, Guangdong province-based trading company, said that beyond food products, China's demand for imported integrated circuits has continued to grow, fueled by the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure and rising demand from the country's electronics manufacturing sector. The Chinese company imported 10.31 billion yuan worth of integrated circuits from the US in the first three quarters, up 74.2 percent year-on-year, statistics from Huangpu Customs in Guangdong showed. Miao Yingchun, a researcher at Wuhan University's Institute for International Studies in Wuhan, Hubei province, said China's demand for US products is being driven by both consumption and production — consumers seeking a wider range of quality goods and manufacturers requiring raw materials, components and equipment. Wang Huiyao, president of the Beijing-based think tank Center for China and Globalization, noted that the Chinese and US economies are deeply interconnected. "If the two countries can expand tariff reductions in specific areas and establish effective trade and investment mechanisms, even relatively limited steps at the outset could help strengthen confidence and pave the way for broader cooperation," he said. China-US trade rose 5.5 percent year-on-year to $400.84 billion during the January-to-August period, while China's imports from the US grew 3.4 percent year-on-year, data from the General Administration of Customs showed. The resilience of bilateral trade is also reflected in recent research. China's expanding import market continues to offer opportunities for US companies despite shifts in global trade and persistent bilateral economic tensions, according to a new report released in Los Angeles that examines changes in US exports to China and the broader impact of the China International Import Expo. The report, "The Evolution of the Structure of US Exports to China and the Extended Effects Index from a CIIE Perspective (2026)", was released earlier this week at the Bridge to Shanghai: Business Opportunities with China event, part of an overseas outreach series ahead of the ninth CIIE, which will be held in Shanghai from Nov 5 to 10. The report said the composition of trade also points to continuing economic complementarity between the world's two largest economies. It identifies China as the largest overseas market for US soybeans and cotton in 2026, and an important market for US integrated circuits and medical devices. It also said the US remains a major source of China's services imports and has maintained a surplus in bilateral services trade. Those patterns, according to the researchers, underscore the enduring commercial ties between the two economies even as tariffs, technology restrictions and changes in global sourcing have altered the bilateral trade landscape. Li Qingjuan, director of the Think Tank Center at Fudan University's Fudan International School of Finance, said the CIIE is no longer simply about bringing products into the Chinese market. Instead, it has evolved into a global platform for companies to showcase their products, connect with potential partners and explore business opportunities. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Holiday travel, spending boom mirror vitality of China's vast market
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
Holiday travel, spending boom mirror vitality of China's vast market BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- From bustling transport hubs and crowded scenic areas to fully booked restaurants and busy shopping districts, strong travel flows and vibrant consumption during the National Day holiday highlighted the resilience and momentum of China's holiday economy. Data from the Ministry of Transport showed that during this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, known as "Golden Week," cross-regional passenger trips reached 2.14 billion, averaging 306 million a day, slightly above the daily average recorded a year earlier. Longer breaks, richer local experiences, rising inbound travel and policy-supported consumption... What stood out this year was not just the sheer number of travelers, but how the holiday economy was changing shape. LONGER JOURNEYS, DEEPER EXPERIENCES With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays separated by only three working days this year, some travelers took three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day extended holiday. Data from Trip.com Group showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into such a break. That extra stretch has helped reshape travel preferences, driving demand for longer-distance trips, a more relaxed pace and more immersive experiences. Online travel platform Qunar said bookings for flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose by more than 40 percent year on year during the National Day holiday, while hotel bookings involving stays across four or more cities jumped 53 percent year on year. Improved transport links are making long-distance trips more accessible than ever. Before the holiday, new high-speed rail sections, including the Xiong'an-Shangqiu, Xi'an-Ankang, and Harbin-Yichun lines, began operation, connecting more destinations across the country. For families like Wang Lei's from Harbin, who traveled to Yichun to enjoy the autumn scenery, a journey that once took seven hours now takes just over one hour. "The time we used to spend on the road can now be spent enjoying the destination," Wang said. Experts said longer breaks extend the consumption chain and expand spending opportunities, giving transport, hospitality, catering and scenic spots a longer operating window and deeper spending potential. Official data showed that during the National Day holiday, average daily sales in service sectors rose 19.5 percent year on year, with tourism, sightseeing and entertainment services up 23.6 percent, catering services up 9 percent, cultural and arts services up 20.9 percent, and sports services up 29.4 percent year on year. A noticeable shift unfolded during this year's National Day holiday: more travelers are looking beyond big-name cities and turning to smaller counties for their getaways. In Mile City, southwest China's Yunnan Province, tourist Chen Jinhui from Shanghai in east China ordered a cup of local coffee and joined a community concert. "Coming to a small city, basking in the sun and relaxing -- that's the Yunnan way of life," he said. Data from Qunar showed that hotel bookings in popular counties rose 32 percent year on year, with Jiuzhaigou County in southwest China's Sichuan and Burqin County in northwest China's Xinjiang among the most sought-after destinations. In August, nine government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, jointly issued guidelines to energize lower-tier markets and boost county-level consumption. The measures aim to streamline consumption channels, broaden the range of available brands, improve service quality, and create diverse and locally tailored consumption experiences in smaller cities and towns. Small counties are no longer marginal players in the consumption landscape; they are becoming an important source of new domestic demand. McKinsey has projected that by 2030, more than 60 percent of China's personal consumption growth will come from third-tier cities and below, as well as county and rural markets. Inbound tourism also remained robust during the holiday. Data from the National Immigration Administration showed that during the holiday, 682,000 foreign nationals entered China, of whom 505,000 arrived under visa-free policies, up 5.4 percent and 9.2 percent, respectively, from a year earlier. As October arrives, autumn colors are spreading across Zhangjiajie National Forest Park in central China's Hunan Province. Tourists of different nationalities can be seen pausing for photos, listening to guides explain the area's unusual landscape, or watching local Tujia ethnic performances. "Zhangjiajie is beautiful. We walked through the forest, felt close to nature, and it was very relaxing," said Noah, a tourist from Germany. He said he was especially impressed by the Tujia intangible cultural heritage performances and that the warmth of the local people made the visit truly memorable. POLICY TAILWINDS, SMARTER SPENDING Strong storefront demand and supportive policies are boosting consumption momentum. In the first six days of the National Day holiday, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 2.5 percent and 4.7 percent year on year, respectively. Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 33.48 billion yuan (about 4.97 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 6.39 million consumers. "During the holiday, we bought a new refrigerator. The subsidy saved us more than 1,000 yuan," said a Tianjin resident surnamed Wang. The National Development and Reform Commission said before the holiday that it, together with the Ministry of Finance, had allocated the fourth and final batch of 62.5 billion yuan in ultra-long special treasury bonds for consumer goods trade-in programs, bringing this year's total to 250 billion yuan. Data from the Ministry of Commerce showed that from Oct. 1 to 6, sales of embodied AI robots on key platforms surged 130 percent year on year, while sales of smart glasses doubled. In Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, new robots, AI translators and other tech gadgets have become popular purchases among foreign tourists. "The number of overseas visitors has clearly increased. Most of them are buying tech products. Many come empty-handed and leave with full suitcases," said a local shop owner. More international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country firsthand, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. From "China Travel" to "China Haul," the trend not only shows how Chinese manufacturing and innovation are winning over global visitors, but also confirms the potential and resilience of China's vast domestic market, supported by visa-free entry, expanded duty-free shopping and improved tax refund services for international visitors, said Zou Yunhan, a researcher with the State Information Center. item.title: China remains committed to letting market play decisive role in determining exchange rate: central bank
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
China remains committed to letting market play decisive role in determining exchange rate: central bank BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China remains committed to letting market forces play a decisive role in determining the RMB exchange rate, the country's central bank said on Thursday. The People's Bank of China (PBOC) stressed in a statement outlining its view on the RMB exchange rate that the country adopts a managed floating exchange rate regime based on market supply and demand with reference to a basket of currencies. The RMB has moved in both directions since the country's exchange rate regime reform in 2005, said the central bank. In bilateral terms, the RMB has strengthened against the U.S. dollar from 8.27 per dollar in July 2005, when the reform was launched, to around 6.7 per dollar recently, appreciating by 23 percent cumulatively. In multilateral terms, the RMB nominal effective exchange rate calculated by the Bank for International Settlements has appreciated by over 50 percent since the exchange rate regime reform in 2005, while its real effective exchange rate up by 35 percent, according to the PBOC. Since 2025, the RMB has strengthened by about 9 percent against the dollar. In particular, while non-dollar currencies have weakened broadly amid surging dollar index and Treasury yields since 2026, the RMB has extended its upward trend against the dollar. "China has no need or intent to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation, nor has it ever resorted to competitive devaluation," said the central bank. China's trade growth is driven by its growing industrial competitiveness in the global market, said the central bank. Exchange rate dynamics are driven by a number of factors including economic growth, monetary policy, financial market, geopolitics and sudden shocks, the PBOC said, adding that there is no straightforward relationship between the exchange rate and the current account. Regarding global economic imbalances, the PBOC said in the statement that they are deeply intertwined with shifting global division of labor, inherent flaws in the international monetary system, and persistently high fiscal deficits and high consumption in some countries. Addressing global imbalances requires collective actions from all stakeholders, according to the central bank. "Attributing one's decline in industrial competitiveness, weakened fiscal discipline, and complicated structural issues simply to others' exchange rates is nothing but shifting the responsibility for adjustment onto others and dodging accountability," said the central bank. A number of models for assessing the equilibrium exchange rate have emerged from academic studies over the years. Noting that there is no well-established methodology for evaluating the equilibrium level of exchange rates internationally, the central bank said "therefore, citing idiosyncratic assessment findings as 'official evidence' for RMB undervaluation is a misinterpretation and misuse of those findings." The central bank said China has long been a contributor to global economic rebalancing. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China will stay the course in transforming its economic growth model, expand domestic demand, improve the business environment, deepen high-standard opening up, and pursue a more open, inclusive and balanced global economy, the bank said. Lu Lei, deputy governor of the PBOC, said in September that China operates a managed floating exchange rate regime, allowing market forces to play a decisive role in exchange rate determination while guarding against herd behavior and the self-reinforcing effects of irrational expectations. In recent years, as China's export structure has undergone transformation and upgrading, companies have strengthened their pricing power and foreign exchange risk management capabilities, significantly reducing the sensitivity of China's trade to exchange rate movements, Lu said. Meanwhile, foreign trade enterprises have increasingly used foreign exchange hedging instruments, while the RMB's share of trade settlement has continued to rise, further reducing the sensitivity of trade to exchange rate fluctuations, Lu added. Guan Tao, chief economist at Huafu Securities, said that factors supporting both appreciation and depreciation of the RMB are currently at play. In the short term, factors favoring a stronger RMB have the upper hand. Over the longer term, two-way fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate remain the norm, Guan noted. item.title: Coiled embroidery of Tu ethnic group weaves a thriving industry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
Coiled embroidery of Tu ethnic group weaves a thriving industry In Huzhu Tu Autonomous County, Haidong city, northwest China's Qinghai Province, coiled embroidery has been passed down among the Tu people for more than 1,000 years. Today it has grown into a distinctive industry worth more than 27 million yuan (about $4.03 million) a year. Li Faxiu began learning Tu coiled embroidery at 7. Nearly 70 years later, she is a national-level representative inheritor of the craft, working out of the intangible cultural heritage workshop in Danma town. Embroiders work at Li Faxiu's workshop. (People's Daily Online/Kuang Yu) In 1995, she carried her embroidery to Beijing for the Fourth World Conference on Women. At the exhibition, the pieces drew so much attention that she sold every one. "I used to think coiled embroidery was simply something kept in a chest as part of a bride's dowry. Only later did I realize it could also be a good way to make a living," Li said. At the time, many young people in her village had left for work elsewhere, and the women who stayed behind had few ways to earn money beyond farming. Li wondered whether she could get them back to the needles and thread they had set aside. During the farming off-season she traveled from village to village giving free lessons, then set up an intangible cultural heritage workshop that now brings together more than 50 local embroiderers who work whenever they have time and are paid by the piece. The county set up a dedicated company for Tu coiled embroidery in 2007. Seventeen years later, it added an industrial base for the craft. "The company and the base handle product design and market development, while embroiderers across the county are responsible for production," said Ha Chengqing, head of the coiled embroidery industrial base. The county has now trained 75 inheritors of Tu coiled embroidery, along with 5,300 full-time embroiderers and more than 3,000 seasonal ones. Li Faxiu shows a piece of coiled embroidery. (People's Daily Online/Kuang Yu) "This has helped rural women increase their incomes. The highest earners can make 40,000 to 50,000 yuan ($5,937 to 7,421) a year," Ha said. Working with universities and independent design studios, the base has adapted signature coiled embroidery motifs — sunflowers, rainbow patterns — onto designer toys, blind-box charms and other products. "We have developed more than 100 creative cultural products across eight categories, with annual sales exceeding 3 million yuan," Ha said. "During activities that bring intangible cultural heritage into classrooms, primary, secondary and university students have all shown great interest in coiled embroidery. Young people today are well-educated. They can promote the craft, create new designs and lead everyone forward. I hope they will pass coiled embroidery down from generation to generation," Li said. item.title: Flame for Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade lit in Turin
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
Flame for Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade lit in Turin Mayor of Changchun Gu Gang (2nd L) and president of FISU Leonz Eder (1st L) jointly light the cauldron with the torch from the first World University Games in Turin in 1959 during the flame collection ceremony for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Turin, Italy, Oct. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan) TURIN, Italy, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The flame for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade was lit Thursday in Turin, Italy, where the first World University Games were held in 1959, beginning its journey to China ahead of the January event. Changchun Mayor Gu Gang and International University Sports Federation President Leonz Eder jointly lit a cauldron using a torch from the inaugural Games before transferring the flame to a lantern for the Changchun Games. The lantern was carried through central Turin from the University of Turin to the Polytechnic University of Turin, passing the Egyptian Museum along the way. Gu expressed hope that the flame would symbolize friendship and that winter sports would promote cultural exchanges between East and West, fostering mutual understanding among young people worldwide. A welcoming ceremony for the flame is scheduled for October 14 in Changchun, according to the Games' organizing committee. The Winter Universiade will run from January 15 to 25, 2027. Eder recently told Xinhua that preparations were progressing smoothly and expressed confidence that the Games would attract a record number of participating delegations. item.title: Where the Long March began, China's new journey unfolds
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09
Where the Long March began, China's new journey unfolds An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 18, 2026 shows a view of Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province. (Xinhua/Zhou Mi) NANCHANG, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The former ferry crossing is about half an hour's walk from the home of Sun Guanfa, 77, in Yudu, a hilly county in east China's Jiangxi Province. For his father, the journey from this riverbank more than nine decades ago was part of an epic. In October 1934, some 86,000 soldiers of the Red Army crossed the Yudu River to embark on what later came to be known as the Long March. In a country beset by foreign invasion, social turmoil and destitution, the fledgling Red Army, led by the Communist Party of China (CPC), was fighting for national independence and the liberation of the Chinese people. But at the time, it was encircled by the overwhelming and much better-armed Kuomintang forces. What followed was an epic military maneuver: from Yudu, Red Army troops trekked roughly 12,500 kilometers across China, crossing snow-covered mountains and treacherous marshlands, all the while battling enemy forces. They eventually reached the country's northwest, where, in 1936, they were joined by several other Red Army branches, marking the victorious conclusion of the Long March. This military maneuver preserved the Red Army. It also gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. In Yudu, the Long March is not simply a chapter in a history book. It is a family story. More than 17,000 residents joined the departing army. Only 277 were recorded as eventually returning home, said Zhong Min, a guide at a museum built beside the river to commemorate the departure. Her voice still catches when she says that number. Her maternal great-grandfather died fighting the encirclement campaigns. Her husband's grandfather marched away with the troops and was never heard from again. Sun's father fell in a battle that saw the forces of the Red Army reduced to just over 30,000. "We are not telling other people's stories," Zhong said. "We are telling our own families'." Here, the Long March is measured not only in kilometers and battles, but in the people who left home knowing they might never return. For Sun, the legacy of that generation is deeply personal. Under a local tradition, Sun was adopted as the son of the soldier who left the riverbank and never returned, so that the soldier's family line could continue. "People of my father's generation were willing to give their lives so ordinary people could be liberated," Sun said. On the same riverbank in 2019, Chinese President Xi Jinping spoke of what had enabled the Party and the Red Army to come back from the brink of destruction time and again: firm ideals and convictions, and strong willpower. "We must not forget our Party's original aspiration and founding mission," said Xi, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission. The Party's long-stated mission, dating to its founding in 1921, is to seek happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation. During the visit, Xi placed a flower basket at a monument commemorating the Red Army's departure and bowed in tribute. He then walked behind the monument to a railing overlooking the river and stood there for a long while. The river remains. For Xi, it was also a place from which to look ahead to China's future. "We came to this place to revisit what it was like when the Red Army set out," he told local people gathered nearby. "Today we are on a new journey -- to build a modern socialist country. We must carry on the work of those who came before us, gear up anew, and set out once more." That new journey was unfolding against a vastly changed backdrop. When Xi visited Yudu, the nationwide campaign he had launched to combat poverty was entering its final stage. It would culminate in the elimination of absolute poverty in a nation of 1.4 billion. Nearly 100 million rural residents were lifted out of poverty under Xi's "targeted poverty alleviation" campaign, which mobilized the entire Party and the nation. Xi announced the victory, as a key part of building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, in 2021 when the CPC marked its centenary. A drone photo taken on Oct. 2, 2026 shows tourists at a memorial hall marking the departure of the Long March by the Central Red Army in Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province. (Photo by Zeng Xiaomao/Xinhua) During his 2019 visit, Xi saw for himself whether the former revolutionary base areas were on track to meet their poverty-reduction targets. At Sun's home, he walked through the main hall to the backyard and checked the kitchen and the bedrooms. There was rice and cooking oil in the kitchen, and the bathroom was clean. Xi asked about the family's income and how Sun's son and daughter-in-law made a living, where their children went to school, and what the school meals were like. "By the time they grow up, we will have achieved the rejuvenation of our nation," Xi said, pointing to Sun's two grandchildren. China aims to basically realize socialist modernization by 2035 and build a great modern socialist country in all respects by the middle of this century, according to the vision set by the Party. Earlier, at the museum where Zhong served as a guide, Xi had stopped before a map of China made from straw sandals. The display recalled how local people worked through the night to make straw sandals for the soldiers, many of whom fought barefoot. They also dismantled doors, bed boards, roof beams and even timber intended for coffins to build pontoon bridges, helping the soldiers cross the Yudu River. "The country has developed and people's lives have improved, but we must remember where it all came from," Xi said. "We must not forget our revolutionary forefathers and those who died for the revolution, or the people of the old revolutionary base areas." Nowadays, golden waves of selenium-rich rice ripple around the 700-year-old village, and rows of modern vegetable greenhouses stand nearby. In the residential area, white-walled houses with gray-tiled roofs sit amid trees, while pavilions nestle between them. "Now we have wages from working, rent from our guesthouses and dividends from our shares," Sun said. "Our annual income has tripled to more than 200,000 yuan (around 29,000 U.S. dollars)." This file photo taken on Oct. 21, 2020 shows Sun Guanfa (L) introducing local agricultural products to tourists in Tantou Village, Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province. (Xinhua/Wan Xiang) The transformation extends well beyond Yudu. Much of southern Jiangxi, once cut off from the outside world by rugged mountains, is far more connected. High-speed rail links it with the city of Shenzhen, the country's economic powerhouse close to Hong Kong. Expressways also reach every county, and paved roads now extend into villages. For local business owners, it no longer means spending two days and two nights on the road to source a critical part. Now they can hop on a high-speed train, pick up what they need in the morning and return that afternoon, drastically speeding up the development of a prototype. The change is not only about getting around. Industries such as non-ferrous metals and advanced materials, electronics and information technology, and textiles and apparel have taken root here. For ordinary people, the changes are closer to home. Housing has improved, drinking water is safer, and schools and medical care are more accessible. More people can now earn a living without leaving their hometowns. In March, the Hong Kong Polytechnic University launched a facility dedicated to research into smart wearables and smart clothing in Xingguo, a county next to Yudu. This summer, Yudu welcomed students from more than 170 universities across China who came to retrace the Long March at the places where it began. Many realized that the Red Army soldiers who set out were their age. "Standing where those young soldiers began their journey gave me a deeper understanding of what they accomplished," said Liu Fanshuo, an undergraduate studying automation. Today, five modern bridges span the Yudu River near the crossings where local people once built pontoon bridges to help the Red Army cross. On the banks, Sun pours hot tea for tourists whose lives might have been very different had those soldiers never crossed. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
